items.q: Which sequence of locations does the labeled protein most likely pass through, according to the graph?
options: Rough ER, then Golgi complex, then secretory vesicles, then outside the cell
Golgi complex, then rough ER, then secretory vesicles, then outside the cell
Rough ER, then secretory vesicles, then Golgi complex, then outside the cell
Rough ER, then outside the cell, with the Golgi and vesicles filling up afterward

items.q: At 40 minutes, what percentage of the labeled protein is in the Golgi complex and the secretory vesicles combined? Give a whole number.
The experiment is repeated with a drug that stops vesicles from budding off the Golgi complex. Which result at 90 minutes is most likely?
options: Most label is still in the rough ER, because proteins pile up in the ER when the Golgi is blocked
Most label is in the Golgi complex, and very little is outside the cell
Most label is outside the cell, because proteins leak out of the Golgi
Most label is in secretory vesicles, which pile up beside the membrane

items.q: A student claims the protein is built in the Golgi complex and then sent to the rough ER to be stored. Which evidence from the graph best refutes this claim?
options: The share of label outside the cell rises steadily from 40 to 120 minutes.
The rough ER holds 90% of the label at 0 minutes, and its share falls as the Golgi's share rises.
Secretory vesicles hold more label at 60 minutes than the Golgi complex does.
The rough ER still holds a small share of the label at 120 minutes, long after the Golgi has emptied.

items.q: Why does the labeled protein appear in the rough ER within minutes, instead of first collecting in the cytosol?
options: The rough ER makes its own amino acids and builds proteins from them without ribosomes.
Ribosomes in the nucleus build the protein and pass it straight into the ER.
Ribosomes bound to the rough ER build it and thread it into the ER as it grows.
Free ribosomes build the protein, and the finished protein later moves into the ER.

items.q: Cell X comes from the liver. The animal is then given a daily dose of a drug that liver cells break down. After two weeks, which change in cell X is most likely?
options: The smooth ER takes up a larger share of the cell's volume.
The lysosomes take up a larger share of the cell's volume.
The rough ER takes up a larger share of the cell's volume.
The mitochondria shrink, because breaking down drugs releases energy.

items.q: How many times larger is the share of cell volume taken up by mitochondria in cell Y than in cell Z? Give your answer to one decimal place.

options: Cell Y makes most of the animal's exported proteins, because mitochondria build proteins for export.
Cell Y uses ATP at a high, steady pace, because mitochondria make most of a cell's ATP.
Cell Y stores most of the animal's lipids, because mitochondria are where lipids are made.
Cell Y breaks down large amounts of engulfed material, because mitochondria digest worn-out parts.

items.q: A researcher suspects that cell Z engulfs bacteria and digests them. Which further observation would most strengthen this claim?
options: Cell Z has more free ribosomes per cell than cell W, which exports large amounts of protein.
Cell Z is larger in total volume than any of the other three cell types.
Micrographs of cell Z show bacteria inside vesicles that have fused with lysosomes.
Cell Z has a smaller share of mitochondria than cell X or cell Y.

items.q: Which statement best describes the data?
options: The enzyme breaks down protein fastest at pH 7.2, the pH of the cytosol.
The enzyme breaks down protein fastest near pH 4.5 to 5.0 and very slowly at pH 7.2.
The amount of protein broken down rises steadily as the pH rises from 3.5 to 7.2.
The enzyme breaks down about the same amount of protein at each pH that the students tested.

items.q: At the pH of the cytosol, the enzyme works at what percentage of its fastest measured pace? Give a whole number.
If a lysosome leaks a few enzyme molecules into the cytosol, the cell is usually not harmed. Which explanation is best supported by the data?
options: At the cytosol's pH of 7.2, the enzyme works at under a tenth of its fastest pace.
The cytosol is more acidic than the lysosome, and the enzyme does not work in acid.
Proteins in the cytosol are made of different amino acids from those the enzyme attacks.
The enzyme works faster in the cytosol, so it finishes its job before it reaches anything important.

items.q: A drug raises the pH inside lysosomes from about 4.8 to about 7.0. What is the most likely result after several days?
options: Worn-out organelles break down faster, so the cell has fewer lysosomes.
The enzymes leave the lysosomes and digest the cytosol, killing the cell within minutes.
Undigested material builds up inside the lysosomes, which swell.
The cell stops making the enzyme, because it is no longer needed.

items.q: A biologist finds working ribosomes inside the mitochondria of a muscle cell. Which statement best explains this finding?
options: The ribosomes wandered in from the cytosol to help the mitochondrion take in fuel.
Mitochondria have their own DNA and ribosomes and build some of their own proteins.
Ribosomes inside mitochondria break down worn-out proteins, as lysosomes do.
The ribosomes were made by the mitochondrion's own rough ER and stored there for later use.

items.q: Two mitochondria are the same size, but the inner membrane of one has many more cristae. Which prediction is best?
options: The one with fewer cristae makes ATP faster, because its matrix has more room for the reactions that need space.
Both make ATP at the same pace, because they are the same size.
The one with more cristae makes ATP faster: more inner membrane holds more ATP-making proteins.
The one with more cristae makes more DNA, because the DNA is stored in the folds.

items.q: Put the steps in the order a secreted protein follows, from its gene to outside the cell.
options: mRNA carrying the gene's instructions leaves the nucleus through a nuclear pore.
A ribosome on the rough ER builds the protein and threads it into the ER.
A vesicle buds off the ER and carries the protein to the Golgi complex.
The Golgi modifies the protein and packages it into a new vesicle.
The vesicle fuses with the cell membrane and releases the protein outside.

items.q: A drug takes apart microtubules in cells that secrete a protein. Which effect is most likely?
options: Ribosomes stop linking amino acids, so no protein is made.
Fewer vesicles reach the cell membrane, so less protein is released.
The Golgi complex moves to the nucleus and fuses with it.
The cell membrane falls apart, so the protein leaks out faster.

items.q: What is the main job of the nucleolus?
options: It makes rRNA and assembles the pieces of ribosomes.
It stores the cell's ATP until it is needed.
It packages proteins into vesicles for export.
It breaks down worn-out organelles.

items.q: In a rare disorder, cells lack one lysosomal enzyme that breaks down a particular lipid. Which result would you predict in these cells?
options: The lipid is broken down in the mitochondria instead, so nothing builds up.
The smooth ER stops making lipids, so the lipid disappears from the cell.
The lipid builds up inside lysosomes, and the lysosomes swell.
The lipid is exported faster through the Golgi complex.

Acid reaches the same depth in each cube, so it reaches a smaller share of a larger cube.
Acid reaches a smaller depth in large cubes, because their surface area ÷ volume is lower.
Acid reaches the whole volume of each cube, but large cubes take longer to turn clear.

items.q: A student also soaks a flat slab of the same agar, 4 cm × 4 cm × 0.5 cm, which has the same volume as the 2 cm cube. Predict the result after 10 minutes in the same vinegar.
options: About 78% of the slab turns clear, the same share as the 2 cm cube, because the volumes are equal.
Nearly the whole slab turns clear, because no point in it is more than 0.25 cm from a face.
Less of the slab turns clear than of the 2 cm cube, because the slab has a lower surface area ÷ volume.
Little of the slab turns clear, because acid enters mainly through the narrow edges of a flat shape.

items.q: Which statement best describes the data in the graph?
options: Larger mammals use more oxygen per gram of body mass than smaller mammals do at rest.
Oxygen use per gram falls as body mass rises, steeply among the smallest mammals.
Oxygen use per gram falls by the same amount from each mammal to the next.
Oxygen use per gram is about the same in each of the seven mammals shown.

items.q: How much oxygen, in mL, does a whole 4 g shrew use in one hour at rest? Give your answer to one decimal place.
Which explanation best accounts for the shrew's high oxygen use per gram?
options: Its body has a high surface area ÷ volume, so it loses heat fast for its mass and releases more heat per gram by respiration.
Its cells are much larger than an elephant's cells, so oxygen has to travel much farther inside each one to reach the mitochondria.
Its small body holds less heat, so it needs less oxygen to keep warm than a large animal does.
Its small lungs take in oxygen slowly, so it has to breathe in more of it per gram of body mass to catch up with demand.

items.q: A student says the graph shows that an elephant uses less oxygen each hour than a mouse. Which response is correct?
options: The student is right: the elephant's bar is about one twenty-fifth as tall as the bar for the mouse.
The student is right, because larger animals have a lower surface area ÷ volume and so need less oxygen in total.
Wrong: the graph gives use per gram, and the elephant's far greater mass makes its total far larger.
The student is wrong, because the graph shows the elephant uses more oxygen per gram than the mouse.

items.q: A 25 g lizard, an ectotherm, rests at the same air temperature as the mouse. Predict its oxygen use per gram compared with the mouse's.
options: Much lower, because it does not burn fuel to keep its body warm.
About the same, because the two animals have the same mass.
Much higher, because ectotherms lose heat faster than endotherms.
Higher, because a lizard's scaly skin gives it a larger surface area ÷ volume than a mouse.

items.q: A spherical cell grows until its radius has doubled, keeping the same shape. What happens to its surface area ÷ volume?
options: It doubles, because both surface area and volume grow with size.
It stays the same, because the cell keeps its shape.
It halves, because surface area rises 4 times and volume rises 8 times.
It falls to a quarter, because volume rises 4 times faster than surface area.

Which of these features increase the surface area available for exchange relative to the volume it serves? Select all that apply.
options: Root hairs growing out from cells at the surface of a root
Cells becoming rounder and larger as a tissue grows
Microvilli on the cells lining the small intestine
A thicker layer of cells between the air in the lungs and the blood
A few large air sacs in the lungs replacing many small ones

items.q: In emphysema, the thin walls between neighboring alveoli break down, so many small air sacs merge into fewer, larger ones. Which effect follows most directly?
options: More oxygen enters the blood with each breath, because the larger air sacs hold more air at once.
Less oxygen enters the blood with each breath, because there is less surface for exchange.
Oxygen enters the blood at the same pace, because the lungs hold the same volume of air.
Oxygen stops entering the blood, because larger sacs have no thin walls left for exchange.

items.q: Why can a single cell not keep growing larger and larger?
options: Its volume, and so its need for materials, grows faster than its surface.
Its membrane runs out of phospholipids once the cell reaches a set size.
Larger cells take in materials faster, so they would soon run out of nearby nutrients.
Its DNA stops working properly once the cell grows past a set diameter.

items.q: On hot days, African elephants flap their very large, thin ears, which are full of blood vessels. How do the ears help the elephant?
options: They add a lot of surface for little volume, so heat leaves the blood faster.
They make the elephant look larger to predators, so it can rest more and use less oxygen per gram.
They store extra water, which the elephant draws on to keep its blood cool on hot days.
They lower the elephant's volume, which lowers its body temperature.

items.q: On cold nights, small birds often huddle together in a tight group. Predict how huddling affects each bird's oxygen use.
options: It rises, because the birds keep shifting and moving to stay close together in the group.
It falls, because each bird has less surface exposed to cold air and loses heat more slowly.
It stays the same, because each bird's own surface area ÷ volume does not change.
It rises, because the group shares the oxygen in the air between them.

items.q: Which statement correctly describes diffusion?
options: Particles spread from where they are crowded to where they are sparse.
Particles are moved by the cell from where they are sparse to where they are crowded.
Particles move toward the center of a cell, because the center of the cell has the most room.
Particles stop moving once they reach the side of a container where they are crowded.

items.q: In a version of the agar-cube experiment, a student soaked a 1 cm cube in vinegar for 10 minutes and a 3 cm cube for 20 minutes, then compared the share of each cube that turned clear. What is the main problem with this design?
options: The cubes should have been made of different agar, so that size was not the sole difference.
Soaking time differed, so any difference in results could come from time rather than size.
Two cube sizes are too many to compare in one experiment.
The 3 cm cube should have been soaked for less time, because it is larger.

items.q: Which statement best describes the results?
options: Mixing reached 92% of cells by 40 minutes at 37 °C but stayed near zero at 15 °C.
Labels mixed at about the same pace at both temperatures, each reaching roughly 50% of cells by 20 minutes.
Labels mixed faster at 15 °C than at 37 °C over the first 10 minutes.
Labels mixed in about half of the fused cells at each temperature by 40 minutes.

items.q: At 37 °C, by how many percentage points per minute did the share of fully mixed cells rise between 10 and 30 minutes? Give your answer to one decimal place.
Which explanation best accounts for the difference between the two temperatures?
options: At 15 °C the cold denatures the labeled proteins, so their fluorescent tags fade and are no longer counted as mixed.
At 37 °C the bilayer is fluid and proteins slide sideways; at 15 °C tightly packed lipids hold them.
At 37 °C the fused cell builds new copies of each protein over its whole surface, and this looks like mixing.
At 15 °C the two halves of the fused membrane fail to join, so the two labels stay on separate sides.

items.q: A skeptic argues that the colors mix because the fused cell keeps making new labeled proteins and inserting them everywhere, not because existing proteins move. Which follow-up test would best address this?
options: Repeat at 37 °C with a drug that stops ribosomes making protein.
Repeat the 15 °C experiment for a much longer time, up to two hours, and count again.
Repeat the experiment with two mouse cells that both carry the green label.
Repeat the experiment at 25 °C to see whether the curve lies between the others.

items.q: The 15 °C experiment is repeated with cells whose membranes have been loaded with extra cholesterol. Predict the result compared with the original 15 °C curve.
options: Less mixing, because cholesterol makes membranes stiffer whatever the temperature is.
Somewhat more, because cholesterol keeps the tails from packing tightly in the cold.
Hardly any mixing, because the extra cholesterol binds to the labeled proteins and holds them still.
Mixing at the 37 °C pace, because cholesterol warms the membrane.

items.q: Which statement best describes the data in the table?
options: As growth temperature rises, both the share of unsaturated fatty acids and the fluidity rise.
Unsaturated fatty acids fall as temperature rises, while fluidity stays about the same.
As growth temperature rises, fluidity falls steadily from 0.52 to 0.38.
The share of unsaturated fatty acids is about the same at each of the four temperatures tested.

items.q: Calculate the percent change in the share of unsaturated fatty acids from 15 °C to 43 °C. Give a whole number, with a minus sign if it is a decrease.
Why does a membrane with more unsaturated fatty acids stay fluid at 15 °C?
options: Unsaturated tails are more hydrophilic, so they attract water into the bilayer and loosen it.
Double bonds put kinks in the tails, so the tails do not pack tightly.
Unsaturated tails are longer than saturated ones, so they wave about more and push the heads apart.
Unsaturated tails form hydrogen bonds with each other, which hold the bilayer loosely.

items.q: A laboratory strain of this bacterium has lost the ability to change its fatty acid mix: its membranes stay at about 45% unsaturated fatty acids, the 37 °C value, at any growth temperature. Predict what happens when it is moved from 37 °C to 15 °C.
options: Its membrane stays as fluid as the normal strain's, because temperature has little effect on fatty acid tails.
Its membrane becomes much more fluid, because saturated tails spread apart in the cold.
Its membrane stiffens, so its membrane proteins work poorly and growth slows.
Its membrane gains unsaturated fatty acids from the cold, so nothing changes.

items.q: A student claims that these bacteria change their membrane lipids in a way that keeps membrane fluidity within a narrow range. Which evidence best supports the claim?
options: Fluidity stays at 0.50 to 0.53 while the lipid mix changes from 68% to 38% unsaturated.
The bacteria grew well at each of the four temperatures in the table, from 15 °C up to 43 °C.
The share of unsaturated fatty acids at 15 °C is 68%, the highest in the table.
Each value in the table is the mean of three cultures.

items.q: In a plasma membrane, how are the phospholipids arranged?
options: Two layers: tails meet in the middle, heads face the water on each side
Two layers: hydrophilic heads face each other in the middle, and the tails face the water on each side
In one layer, with heads facing the cytoplasm and tails facing the outside
In a single sheet, with heads and tails alternating side by side

items.q: A transmembrane protein crosses the bilayer once. Which amino acids are most likely in the stretch of the protein that lies inside the bilayer?
options: Amino acids with charged side chains, which attract the phosphate heads
Nonpolar amino acids, which sit well among the hydrophobic tails
Amino acids with polar side chains, which form hydrogen bonds with the tails
Any mix of amino acids, because the inside of the bilayer has little effect on which side chains fit there

items.q: In a membrane protein, one nonpolar amino acid in the stretch that crosses the bilayer is replaced by a charged amino acid. Which result is most likely?
options: The protein sits more firmly in the bilayer, because charges attract the tails.
The protein sits less stably in the bilayer and may not insert properly.
The protein moves to the nucleus, because charged proteins bind DNA.
The protein is unchanged, because one amino acid is too small to matter.

items.q: Which jobs are done by proteins in the plasma membrane? Select all that apply.
options: Moving particular substances across the membrane
Binding a signaling molecule and changing the cell's activity
Letting cells recognize each other
Storing the instructions for building other proteins
Making the phospholipid tails hydrophilic
Holding the two layers of heads together with covalent bonds

items.q: Sugar chains are added to a glycoprotein inside the ER and Golgi. Which side of the plasma membrane do those chains end up on, and why?
options: The cytoplasm side, because the sugars are added in the cytoplasm.
Outside, because a vesicle's inner face becomes the cell's outer face when it fuses.
Both sides equally, because glycoproteins flip over freely in the bilayer.
The outside, because sugar chains are hydrophobic, so the watery cytoplasm pushes them out of the cell.

items.q: A signaling molecule that is too large and too polar to cross the membrane changes the activity of liver cells but has no effect on skin cells. Which explanation is best?
options: Liver cells have surface receptors that bind it; skin cells lack them.
Skin cells have a much thicker plasma membrane, which the molecule is unable to get through.
The molecule is broken down in the blood by enzymes before it can travel as far as the skin.
Liver cells are larger, so the molecule is more likely to hit them.

items.q: How does cholesterol affect an animal cell's membrane at body temperature and above?
options: It restrains phospholipid movement, so the membrane is not too fluid.
It speeds up the movement of phospholipids, making the membrane more fluid.
It replaces proteins in the membrane, so the membrane carries fewer of them.
It forms a separate third layer between the two layers of phospholipids, stiffening the whole membrane.

items.q: A culture of animal cells is warmed from 20 °C to 35 °C. Predict how each quantity changes.

variables.name: Fluidity of the plasma membrane
Speed at which membrane proteins slide sideways
Number of phospholipid layers in the membrane

items.q: One membrane protein can be washed off a membrane with a mild salt solution. Another comes off only when a detergent breaks up the bilayer. What do these results suggest?
options: The first is peripheral, at the surface; the second is integral, embedded in the bilayer.
The first is an integral protein; the second is a peripheral protein.
Both are peripheral proteins held at the surface, but the second is much larger and heavier than the first.
Both are integral proteins, but the first is made of fewer amino acids.

items.q: What does the name "fluid mosaic model" describe?
options: Lipids and proteins that move sideways, with many kinds of proteins scattered through
A membrane made of a liquid layer of water between two protein sheets
A membrane whose proteins are fixed in a regular pattern, like tiles
A membrane that keeps flowing away from the cell and is rebuilt from scratch within a few seconds

items.q: Which statement best describes the pattern in the table?
options: The smallest substances cross fastest, whatever their charge or polarity, and the largest cross slowest.
Nonpolar CO₂ crosses fastest, uncharged polar molecules slower, ions slowest.
Charged ions cross faster than uncharged polar molecules of a similar size.
Molecules with a molar mass above 50 g/mol barely cross a bilayer, whatever their polarity.

items.q: Water crosses the bilayer about 10 to the power of what number times faster than glucose? (For example, 100 times faster would be 10², so the answer would be 2.)
A student claims that a molecule's size alone decides how fast it crosses a phospholipid bilayer. Which comparison from the table best refutes this claim?
options: Glucose (180 g/mol) crosses about ten thousand times more slowly than glycerol (92 g/mol).
Na⁺ (23 g/mol) crosses about 100 times slower than glucose (180 g/mol).
Glycerol (92 g/mol) crosses about a thousand times more slowly than water (18 g/mol).
Water crosses faster than urea, which is three times heavier.

items.q: Why do sodium and chloride ions cross the bilayer so slowly even though they are very small?
options: Their charge keeps them out of the bilayer's hydrophobic core.
They are too heavy to slip between the closely packed phospholipid heads on each surface.
They bind tightly to the phospholipid tails and get stuck partway through the bilayer.
They react with the phosphate heads and are turned into other molecules.

items.q: Intestinal cells take up large amounts of glucose every few minutes after a meal. Based on the table, what must these cells have?
options: Thicker plasma membranes, so more glucose can dissolve in the bilayer.
Transport proteins in the plasma membrane that let glucose cross.
Membranes with fewer phospholipids, so glucose has a shorter path to cross.
A higher share of cholesterol, which attracts glucose into the bilayer.

items.q: Which statement best describes the results?
options: The three groups swelled at about the same pace for the first 3 minutes, then the aquaporin group burst.
Aquaporin oocytes swelled far faster than controls; mercury slowed them.
Mercury made oocytes with aquaporin swell faster than those without it.
Control oocytes swelled fastest, because they had extra water injected.

items.q: Calculate the rate at which the relative volume of the aquaporin oocytes rose between 0 and 3 minutes, in relative units per minute. Give your answer to two decimal places.
Why did the researchers inject the control oocytes with plain water instead of leaving them uninjected?
options: So that the mRNA is the only difference between the two groups.
So that the control oocytes would swell about as fast as the oocytes that were given aquaporin mRNA.
So that the control oocytes would make a small amount of aquaporin too.
So that the control oocytes would start the experiment at a larger volume.

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the fast swelling of the aquaporin oocytes?
options: The injected mRNA made the oocytes' contents much more concentrated, so much more water rushed in after the move.
Ribosomes used the mRNA to make aquaporin, which entered the plasma membrane and let water in faster.
The mRNA itself sat in the plasma membrane and formed holes for water.
The mRNA broke down the phospholipids, so the bilayer let everything through.

items.q: The null hypothesis was that aquaporin has no effect on how fast water enters an oocyte. Which conclusion do the data support?
options: Fail to reject the null hypothesis, because the control oocytes also swelled during the five minutes.
Reject it: aquaporin oocytes swelled far faster, and mercury slowed them.
Reject the null hypothesis, because the mercury-treated oocytes swelled slightly faster than the controls did.
Fail to reject the null hypothesis, because the aquaporin oocytes burst before 5 minutes.

items.q: Which statement best describes the results?
options: Penicillin killed most of the cells in both media, with or without the added sucrose.
Penicillin cut intact cells sharply in dilute medium but not with sucrose.
Sucrose killed most cells, whether or not penicillin was present.
Neither penicillin nor sucrose changed the number of intact cells.

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the penicillin results?
options: Water enters cells in dilute medium; weak walls fail to hold, so cells burst. Sucrose outside keeps water out.
Penicillin dissolves the plasma membrane of the bacteria, and the sucrose in the medium repairs the damaged membrane.
The sucrose feeds the cells, giving them the energy they need to break down the penicillin before it can act.
In dilute medium penicillin enters cells faster and poisons their ribosomes.

items.q: Why was it important to include the group grown in sucrose medium without penicillin?
options: To show that sucrose by itself does not harm the cells.
To make the penicillin work faster in the sucrose medium.
To give the experiment a larger sample size.
To show that sucrose by itself makes the cells lose their rod shape and turn round.

items.q: Penicillin is used to treat bacterial infections in people. Why does it harm the bacteria but not the patient's own cells?
options: Human cells have no peptidoglycan wall for it to act on.
Human cells have thick cell walls made of cellulose, which penicillin is unable to weaken.
Human blood is about as concentrated as the sucrose medium, so human cells take in no water.
Human cells break penicillin down immediately with their lysosomes.

items.q: Which of these need a transport protein to cross a plasma membrane at a useful rate? Select all that apply.
options: Potassium ions (K⁺)
Oxygen (O₂)
Glucose
Carbon dioxide (CO₂)
A steroid hormone such as estrogen
Nitrogen gas (N₂)

items.q: Estrogen, a steroid hormone, acts on cells by binding a receptor inside the cell, while insulin, a protein hormone, binds a receptor on the cell surface. Which explanation fits these facts?
options: Estrogen is a large, charged molecule that is pulled into the cell, while insulin is too small to be held inside.
Estrogen is a lipid that diffuses through the bilayer; insulin is large and polar.
Estrogen enters through aquaporins, while insulin is too large for them.
Estrogen is made inside the same cell it acts on, so it does not have to cross any membrane to reach its receptor.

items.q: A plant cell and an animal cell are both placed in pure water, and water moves into each. What happens next?
options: Both cells burst within a few minutes, because nothing stops the water from continuing to enter.
The plant cell's wall stops its swelling; the animal cell may burst.
The animal cell swells until its cholesterol stops it; the plant cell bursts.
Neither cell changes, because water is unable to cross a plasma membrane made of phospholipids.

items.q: A drug blocks the aquaporins in a kidney cell's plasma membrane. Predict how each quantity changes.

variables.name: Rate at which water crosses the plasma membrane
Rate at which oxygen crosses the plasma membrane
Rate at which carbon dioxide crosses the plasma membrane

items.q: A cell keeps a high concentration of proteins and glucose inside while oxygen moves freely in and out. Which property of the plasma membrane makes this possible?
options: It is selectively permeable: some substances cross easily, others hardly.
It is impermeable to each substance except water, which passes through freely in both directions.
It is fully permeable, but proteins and glucose are too heavy to move across it.
It is permeable to everything at first and then closes.

items.q: Which list correctly matches each group with the main material of its cell wall?
options: Plants: cellulose. Fungi: chitin. Bacteria: peptidoglycan.
Plants: chitin. Fungi: cellulose. Bacteria: peptidoglycan.
Plants: peptidoglycan. Fungi: chitin. Bacteria: cellulose.
Plants: cellulose. Fungi: peptidoglycan. Bacteria: chitin.

items.q: Why did the bag turn blue-black while the beaker water stayed amber?
options: Starch moved out of the bag and reacted with iodine at the bag's surface.
Iodine diffused into the bag; starch is too large to get out.
The cell-like bag used energy to pull iodine inside.
Glucose leaving the bag dragged iodine molecules along with it in the opposite direction, into the bag.

items.q: The bag is left in the beaker for 24 hours. Predict the state of the glucose at the end.
options: Almost the whole of the glucose has left the bag and ended up in the much larger beaker.
Equal concentrations, with molecules still crossing both ways.
Glucose concentration is about equal inside and out, and the glucose molecules have stopped crossing the tubing.
Glucose has moved back into the bag, where it is now more concentrated.

items.q: Which kind of transport moved glucose and iodine in this experiment?
options: Passive transport: each moved down its own gradient.
Active transport, because the two substances moved in opposite directions across the same tubing at the same time.
Bulk transport, because the bag took in iodine in vesicles.
Active transport, because the movement continued for 30 minutes.

items.q: The bag is often used as a model of a cell. Which is the most important way the model differs from a real plasma membrane?
options: Tubing sorts by size alone; a membrane sorts by polarity, charge and its proteins.
The tubing is selectively permeable, while a plasma membrane lets each kind of substance through freely.
The tubing lets water through, while a plasma membrane keeps water out.
The tubing has a much thicker wall than a membrane, so diffusion through it takes several days.

items.q: Which statement best describes the data?
options: In both batches the inside concentration rises well above the outside concentration within the hour.
Untreated cells reach about ten times the outside level; cyanide-treated cells level off at equal.
With cyanide the cells take up the amino acid faster, then stop at a ratio of 1.0.
Without cyanide the ratio levels off at 1.0 after about 30 minutes.

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the difference between the two batches?
options: Cyanide damages the bilayer of the cells, so the amino acid leaks back out as fast as it comes in.
Untreated cells use ATP to move it against its gradient; without ATP it moves only until both sides are equal.
Cyanide makes the outside concentration of the amino acid rise, so the ratio stays at or below 1.0.
The untreated cells make new amino acid of this kind inside, which raises the concentration measured inside.

items.q: At 10 minutes the ratios are 2.1 ± 0.3 without cyanide and 0.6 ± 0.1 with cyanide (±2 SE). What can you conclude?
options: No overlap, so the difference is likely real.
The error bars overlap, so the batches are the same at 10 minutes.
The error bars do not overlap, so there is certainly no difference.
Nothing can be concluded, because error bars matter just for the last time point of a time course.

items.q: The outside concentration of the amino acid is 0.50 mM. What is the concentration inside the untreated cells at 60 minutes, in mM? Give your answer to one decimal place.
At 60 minutes, cyanide is added to the untreated cells. Predict how their ratio changes over the next hour.
options: It stays at about 9.6, because the amino acid already inside is trapped there by the membrane.
It keeps rising, because the cells have stored ATP for the transport.
It falls toward 1.0 as the amino acid leaks out down its gradient.
It drops to 0 at once, because cyanide destroys the amino acid.

items.q: Which statement best describes the data at 37 °C?
options: Healthy cells and cells with no working receptor took in about the same amount of LDL.
Healthy cells took in about 25 times as much LDL as cells with no working receptor.
Cells with no working receptor bound more LDL to their surface than healthy cells.
Healthy cells bound more LDL at 37 °C than at 4 °C.

items.q: Healthy cells at 4 °C have a lot of LDL on their surface but very little inside. Which explanation is best?
options: At 4 °C the LDL receptors are destroyed by the cold, so LDL sticks loosely to the bilayer instead of to receptors.
LDL binds its receptors, but in the cold no vesicles form to take it in.
At 4 °C LDL diffuses straight through the bilayer and out the other side.
At 4 °C the cells use active transport to push LDL back out.

items.q: Predict the level of LDL cholesterol in the blood of the person whose cells lack a working LDL receptor.
options: Lower than normal, because their cells take in LDL by other routes faster.
Higher than normal, because their cells remove little LDL from the blood.
Normal, because LDL is removed from the blood by diffusion anyway.
Lower than normal, because LDL that is not taken in breaks down in the blood.

items.q: What does the 4 °C treatment add to the experiment?
options: It separates binding from uptake: binding works in the cold, uptake does not.
It acts as a negative control by killing the cells.
It doubles the sample size of the experiment, which makes the results at 37 °C more reliable.
It shows that LDL is made by the cells at low temperature.

items.q: Which of these is an example of passive transport? Select all that apply.
options: Oxygen moving from the lungs' air sacs into the blood
A white blood cell engulfing a bacterium
A pancreas cell releasing insulin from vesicles
Root cells taking in potassium from soil water where potassium is much scarcer than inside the cells

items.q: Root cells contain potassium at about 100 times the concentration in the surrounding soil water. What does this tell you about how the cells take in potassium?
options: They take it in by diffusion, because potassium ions are small enough to slip through the bilayer quickly.
By active transport, using ATP to move it against its gradient.
They take it in by exocytosis, in vesicles from the soil.
They take it in through aquaporins, along with water.

items.q: A gland cell releases large amounts of protein by exocytosis but, in an experiment, its endocytosis is blocked. Predict what happens to the cell's surface over time.
options: The surface grows, because each fused vesicle adds its membrane to it.
The plasma membrane shrinks, because each vesicle removes a patch of membrane as it leaves.
The plasma membrane stays the same size, because vesicles release their contents without fusing with it.
The plasma membrane becomes thicker, because vesicles stack on top of it.

items.q: A cell folds its membrane inward around droplets of fluid and pinches them off in small vesicles, taking in whatever is dissolved in the fluid. What is this process called?
options: Pinocytosis
Phagocytosis
Exocytosis
Simple diffusion

items.q: A poison stops a cell from making ATP. Predict how each process changes in the next few minutes.

variables.name: Active transport of ions into the cell
Diffusion of oxygen into the cell
Exocytosis of secretory vesicles

items.q: Animal cells keep K⁺ much more concentrated inside than outside and Na⁺ much more concentrated outside than inside. Which explanation is best?
options: The membrane is impermeable to both ions, so the differences were set when the cell first formed and stay put.
Ions leak slowly, and active transport keeps moving them back.
K⁺ is attracted to the inside of the cell and Na⁺ to the outside, so no energy is needed.
Diffusion moves each ion from low to high concentration until the differences form.

items.q: A student says passive transport "uses no energy at all." Which correction is most accurate?
options: Passive transport uses ATP, but less than active transport does.
It needs no energy from the cell; the particles' own motion drives it.
Passive transport is driven by the energy released when small parts of the membrane break down.
Passive transport uses heat from cellular respiration to push particles.

items.q: Which statement best describes the glucose data?
options: Uptake rate rises steeply at low concentrations, then by less and less as concentration grows.
Uptake rate climbs by the same amount with each additional 2 mM of glucose, across the whole range tested.
Uptake rate rises slowly at first and then faster once the concentration passes about 10 mM.
Uptake rate peaks near 10 mM and then falls as more glucose is added outside the cells.

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the difference between the two curves?
options: Glucose uses a limited number of carrier proteins that all become occupied; X diffuses through the bilayer itself.
Glucose is pumped in using ATP, and the cells run short of ATP at high glucose levels, while X needs no energy.
Glucose is too large to fit through the bilayer at high concentrations, while X fits through at any concentration.
Glucose molecules attract one another at high concentrations and slow down, while X molecules stay evenly spread out.

items.q: Calculate the percent increase in the glucose uptake rate when the outside concentration doubles from 10 mM to 20 mM. Round to the nearest whole percent.
The experiment is repeated with cells treated with a drug that permanently blocks half of their glucose carriers. Which prediction is most consistent with the explanation of the curves?
options: The glucose curve levels off at about half its original height; the X curve does not change.
The glucose curve keeps its original ceiling but takes twice the concentration to reach it; the X curve does not change.
Both curves level off at about half their original heights, because the membrane has fewer open routes.
The glucose curve becomes a straight line like X, because the remaining carriers are no longer crowded.

items.q: A student proposes that substance X also uses a carrier, one with so many copies that it never fills up in this range. Which new result would best support the student's idea?
options: Adding a large amount of a molecule shaped like X to the solution slows the uptake of X.
Repeating the experiment at 25 °C instead of 37 °C slows the uptake of X by a small amount.
The uptake of X at 20 mM is twice its uptake at 10 mM, just as in the original data.
Cells given extra glucose take up X at the same rate as cells given no glucose.

items.q: Which change in the table shows an ion moving down its concentration gradient once the pump stopped?
options: Na⁺ inside the cell rose from 12 to 38 mM, because Na⁺ is more concentrated outside.
K⁺ inside the cell fell from 140 to 112 mM, because K⁺ is more concentrated outside.
Na⁺ outside the cell stayed at 145 mM, because Na⁺ is more concentrated inside.
K⁺ outside the cell stayed at 4 mM, because K⁺ moved into the cell from outside.

items.q: Before ouabain, how many times more concentrated was Na⁺ outside the cell than inside? Give your answer to one decimal place.
Which explanation best accounts for the rise in Na⁺ inside the cells after ouabain was added?
options: Na⁺ keeps leaking in through channels down its gradient, but it is no longer moved back out by the pump.
Ouabain opens extra Na⁺ channels in the membrane, so more Na⁺ floods into the cells than before.
The cells begin making Na⁺ from other molecules once they can no longer import it from outside.
The pump runs backward without ATP and carries Na⁺ inward instead of carrying it out of the cell.

items.q: Suppose ouabain had been left on the cells for several hours instead of 60 minutes. Predict how each quantity would compare with its 60-minute value.

variables.name: Na⁺ inside the cell
K⁺ inside the cell
Na⁺ outside the cell
Size of the charge difference across the membrane (how far from zero)

items.q: In these cells before ouabain was added, which movements use energy from ATP directly? Select all that apply.
options: Na⁺ leaving the cell through the sodium-potassium pump
Na⁺ entering the cell through open sodium channels
K⁺ leaving the cell through open potassium channels
Water entering the cell through aquaporins
Glucose entering the cell through a glucose carrier

items.q: Which feature separates a carrier protein from a channel protein?
options: A carrier binds the substance and changes shape to move it across the membrane.
A carrier moves its substance from low concentration to high concentration.
A carrier uses ATP each time it moves a molecule across the membrane.
A carrier lets any small molecule through, while a channel is specific.

items.q: Kidney tubule cells reabsorb large volumes of water. Some people inherit a faulty aquaporin that does not reach the cell membrane. Which outcome is expected in those tubule cells?
options: Water crosses their membranes more slowly, because the bilayer alone lets water through slowly.
Water stops crossing their membranes, because water is a polar molecule and is blocked by the bilayer.
Water crosses faster, because the cells switch to pumping water with ATP instead.
Water crosses at the normal rate, because water moves by diffusion and needs no protein.

items.q: Tetrodotoxin, a poison from puffer fish, plugs the voltage-gated sodium channels of nerve cells. Which effect is expected in a poisoned nerve cell?
options: Na⁺ cannot rush in when the membrane voltage changes, so the cell cannot send its normal signal.
Na⁺ is no longer pumped out of the cell, so it builds up inside and the cell slowly swells with water.
Na⁺ rushes into the cell through the blocked channels faster than usual, flooding the inside.
K⁺ can no longer leave the cell, because K⁺ shares the same channels as sodium ions do.

items.q: Inside a resting animal cell the membrane potential is −70 mV and Na⁺ is far more concentrated outside. Which statement correctly describes the electrochemical gradient for Na⁺?
options: Both the concentration difference and the negative inside pull Na⁺ into the cell.
The concentration difference pulls Na⁺ in, but the negative inside pushes it back out.
The two forces cancel each other, which is why Na⁺ needs a pump to enter the cell.
Na⁺ feels no electrical push, because charge affects negatively charged ions but not positive ones.

items.q: One sodium-potassium pump completes 100 cycles per second. How many more positive charges does it move out of the cell than into it each second?
Put the steps of one cycle of the sodium-potassium pump in order, starting with the pump open to the inside of the cell.
options: Three Na⁺ ions from the cytoplasm bind to the pump.
ATP transfers a phosphate group to the pump, and the pump changes shape.
The pump opens to the outside and releases the three Na⁺ ions.
Two K⁺ ions from outside the cell bind to the pump.
The phosphate group comes off, and the pump returns to its first shape, releasing K⁺ inside.

items.q: Liver cells take in glucose through carriers that work by facilitated diffusion. As soon as glucose enters, the cell chemically changes it into a different molecule. How does this affect glucose uptake?
options: It keeps the inside glucose level low, so a gradient into the cell is kept up and uptake continues.
It traps glucose behind the carrier, so the carrier stops working once the first molecules enter.
It gives the carrier the energy it needs to move glucose against its gradient into the cell.
It has no effect, because a carrier moves glucose at a fixed rate that does not depend on concentration.

items.q: A researcher wants to show that a new transport protein moves substance Z by facilitated diffusion rather than by active transport. Which result would be the strongest evidence?
options: Z still enters cells after ATP production is blocked, and net movement stops when inside and outside levels are equal.
Z enters cells faster at higher outside concentrations, and the rate levels off at high concentrations.
Z is a charged molecule that does not cross an artificial membrane made of phospholipids alone, with no protein present.
Z enters cells when the transport protein is present, and blocking the protein stops Z uptake.

items.q: Which of these substances need a transport protein to cross a cell membrane at a useful rate? Select all that apply.
options: Potassium ions (K⁺)
Oxygen gas (O₂)
Carbon dioxide (CO₂)
A small steroid hormone

items.q: In muscle cells, a ligand-gated channel opens when a signaling molecule released by a nerve cell binds to it, and Na⁺ then enters the muscle cell. What does the gate add, compared with a channel that is always open?
options: Control over when the ions flow, so Na⁺ enters only after the signal arrives.
Energy for the ions, so Na⁺ can move against its concentration gradient.
A larger number of channels, so the cell can take in more Na⁺ at rest.
A change in which ion passes, so the channel can carry K⁺ when it is closed.

items.q: Based on the graph, at about what sucrose concentration would potato cores show no net change in mass?
options: About 0.20 mol/L
About 0.35 mol/L
About 0.50 mol/L
About 0.75 mol/L

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the potato cores gaining mass in 0 mol/L sucrose (plain water)?

The cells used ATP to pump water inward until their cell walls stopped them from swelling any further.

Sweet potato cells have a higher water potential than potato cells, because they gain more mass in water.

items.q: A U-shaped tube is divided at the bottom by a membrane that lets water through but not sucrose. Side 1 is filled with 0.1 mol/L sucrose and side 2 with 0.5 mol/L sucrose, to the same height. What happens over the next hour?

Sucrose moves from side 2 to side 1 until both sides hold 0.3 mol/L, and the levels stay equal.

The levels are equal, because both sides began with the same concentration of dissolved solute.
The level is higher on side 1, because glucose molecules are smaller and attract more water.
The levels are equal, because glucose crosses to side 2 and balances the sucrose exactly.

items.q: Paramecium, a single-celled pond organism, was placed in water with added salt. Its contractile vacuole emptied about 12 times per minute in pond water, 6 times in 50 mM salt and 2 times in 100 mM salt. Which explanation fits these data?
options: Saltier water is less hypotonic to the cell, so less water enters and less has to be expelled.
Saltier water is more hypotonic to the cell, so the vacuole has less time to fill between contractions.
Salt enters the cell and blocks the vacuole, so the cell pumps out salt instead of water.
Salt slows the cell's use of ATP, so the vacuole fills with water just as fast but empties more slowly.

items.q: A trout lives in fresh water, which has far fewer solutes than its blood. Which set of responses helps it keep its water balance?
options: It makes large volumes of dilute urine and takes up salts across its gills.
It drinks large volumes of water and gets rid of extra salts through its gills.
It produces small volumes of concentrated urine to keep water in its body.
It keeps the solute concentration of its blood equal to that of the fresh water.

items.q: A patient needs fluid through a drip into a vein. Which fluid would keep the patient's red blood cells at their normal volume? Select all that apply.
options: A salt solution isotonic to blood plasma
Distilled water
A salt solution three times as concentrated as plasma
A glucose solution half as concentrated as plasma

items.q: Grass along a road that was heavily salted in winter often wilts in spring, even when the soil is moist. Which explanation fits?
options: Salt lowers the water potential of the soil water, so less water moves into the roots and some may leave them.
Salt raises the water potential of the soil water, so water moves out of the soil too quickly to reach the roots.
Salt enters the root cells and makes them hypotonic to the soil, so water flows into the roots too fast.
Salt dissolves the cell walls of the roots, so the cells can no longer hold turgor pressure.

items.q: Which of these has the highest water potential?
options: Pure water in an open beaker
A 0.2 mol/L sucrose solution in an open beaker
The cytoplasm of a firm plant cell
A 0.2 mol/L salt solution in an open beaker

items.q: Two solutions are separated by a membrane that lets water through but not glucose, sodium or chloride. Side 1 holds 0.1 mol/L glucose; side 2 holds 0.1 mol/L sodium chloride (NaCl). Which way does water move, and why?
options: Into side 2, because each NaCl unit splits into two ions, so side 2 holds more dissolved particles.
Into side 1, because a glucose molecule is larger than a sodium ion and holds onto more water.
Neither way, because both sides hold the same amount of dissolved substance per liter.
Into side 1, because sodium and chloride ions carry charges that push water molecules away.

items.q: Why can a plant cell take in water from a hypotonic solution without bursting?
options: Its cell wall resists the swelling, and the pressure that builds up stops further net water entry.
Its membrane closes its aquaporins once the cell is full, so no more water can enter it.
Its central vacuole pumps the extra water back out of the cell as fast as it comes in.
Its cytoplasm has a higher water potential than the solution, so water stays outside.

items.q: Which observation shows that, in the control, glucose was moved into the cells against its concentration gradient?

The ratio rises fastest during the first 5 minutes and then more slowly.
The control ratio is higher than the ouabain ratio at each time point after 10 minutes.
The error bars for the control grow larger as the experiment goes on.

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the results when Na⁺ was replaced by choline?
options: With no Na⁺ gradient to drive the cotransporter, glucose entered only passively and stopped at a ratio of 1.
Choline entered the cells through the cotransporter in place of Na⁺, and it carried glucose in more slowly than Na⁺ does.
Without Na⁺ the cells could not make ATP, so the glucose cotransporter had no energy and glucose could not enter.
Choline made the outside solution hypertonic, so water left the cells and glucose became trapped outside them.

items.q: With ouabain, glucose built up for about 10 minutes and then fell back toward a ratio of 1. Which explanation fits best?

Ouabain needed about 10 minutes to enter the cells, and then it blocked the glucose cotransporter directly.
Ouabain stopped the cells from making ATP after 10 minutes, so the cotransporter ran out of the energy it uses directly.
The cells used up the glucose they had taken in for energy, which lowered the inside concentration after 10 minutes.

items.q: Why did the researchers replace Na⁺ with an equal concentration of choline, instead of simply leaving the Na⁺ out?

To give the cells another ion they could use in place of Na⁺ to drive glucose into the cells.
To make sure the sodium-potassium pump had enough K⁺ to keep working at its normal rate.
To raise the electrical charge of the solution, so that glucose would be attracted into the cells.

items.q: In the control, the outside glucose concentration stayed at 5 mM. What was the glucose concentration inside the cells at 30 minutes, in mM?

items.q: Which of these are examples of cotransport (secondary active transport)? Select all that apply.

Glucose entering an intestinal cell together with Na⁺
Na⁺ and K⁺ being exchanged by the sodium-potassium pump
Water entering a leaf cell through aquaporins

items.q: What distinguishes primary active transport from secondary active transport (cotransport)?
options: Primary uses ATP directly; secondary uses the energy stored in a gradient that a pump built.

Primary moves ions; secondary moves large molecules inside vesicles.
Primary needs a transport protein; secondary happens through the lipid bilayer itself.

items.q: Heart muscle cells remove calcium using an exchanger that lets three Na⁺ flow into the cell while it carries one Ca²⁺ out. How is this transporter best described?

A channel: it forms an open tunnel through which both ions pass in whichever direction they are pushed.

items.q: Digoxin partly blocks the sodium-potassium pump in heart muscle cells. Using the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger described above, predict the effect on calcium inside the cells.
options: Calcium inside rises, because a weaker Na⁺ gradient drives less Ca²⁺ out through the exchanger.
Calcium inside falls, because more Na⁺ inside pushes Ca²⁺ out through the exchanger faster.
Calcium inside stays the same, because the exchanger does not use ATP and is unaffected.
Calcium inside falls, because the blocked pump now carries Ca²⁺ out in place of Na⁺.

items.q: The intestinal cotransporter carries 2 Na⁺ in with each glucose. The sodium-potassium pump spends 1 ATP to remove 3 Na⁺. If every Na⁺ that enters with glucose must be pumped back out, how many ATP are spent per glucose taken in? Round to two decimal places.

Glucose gives the intestinal cells ATP that they spend to pump water directly from the gut into the blood.
Glucose binds to Na⁺ in the drink, forming a larger molecule that passes straight through the lipid bilayer.

Glucose built up inside the cell by sodium-glucose cotransport
Entry of a small nonpolar test molecule that the cell does not use, held at a fixed concentration outside

items.q: A cell takes in an amino acid that is already 20 times more concentrated inside than outside. The uptake stops when Na⁺ is removed from the outside solution, but not when the cell's ATP is briefly lowered. Which mechanism do the data point to?

A pump that spends ATP directly to move the amino acid into the cell against its gradient.
Facilitated diffusion through a channel, because the amino acid needs a transport protein.
Endocytosis, because amino acids are too large to cross the membrane through proteins.

items.q: A white blood cell is about to engulf a bacterium. Which mechanism moves the bacterium into the cell? Select all that apply.

Cotransport, with Na⁺ carrying the bacterium in
Facilitated diffusion through a large channel protein
Simple diffusion through the lipid bilayer

items.q: A small, nonpolar molecule is more concentrated outside a cell than inside. Which route will most of it take into the cell?

Facilitated diffusion through a specific carrier protein, because it moves down its gradient
Cotransport with Na⁺, because the cell keeps a steep Na⁺ gradient across its membrane
Active transport by a pump, because the cell controls which molecules may enter it

items.q: In a model of an intestinal cell, the sodium-potassium pump sits on the side facing the blood, and the sodium-glucose cotransporter on the side facing the gut. What happens to glucose uptake from the gut if only the pump on the blood side stops?

It continues unchanged, because the pump and the cotransporter are on different sides of the cell.
It speeds up, because Na⁺ is no longer leaving the cell and is free to carry more glucose in.
It continues unchanged, because the cotransporter uses its own supply of ATP to move glucose.

items.q: Which statement correctly describes the lysosomal enzyme?

It is most active near pH 7 and works poorly in acidic conditions below pH 5.

The lysosomal enzyme becomes more active at pH 7.2, but the cytosol contains nothing it can break down.
The cytosol is more acidic than the lysosome, so the leaked enzyme is quickly destroyed by the acid.

Material in lysosomes is broken down faster, because the cytosolic enzyme now works inside them.
The lysosomal enzymes leak out and begin digesting the cytosol at their highest rate.
Lysosomes work as before, because their enzymes are protected by the lysosome membrane.

The outer membrane has been partly lost in liver cells, so the inner membrane is left to do its job.

The pancreas cell's mitochondrial membranes add up to more than its rough ER.

items.q: What is the nucleoid of a prokaryotic cell?

A membrane-bound sac that holds its DNA, like a small nucleus
A cluster of ribosomes where the cell builds its proteins
The thick outer layer of the cell wall that protects the DNA

items.q: Liver cells build fatty acids in the cytosol and break fatty acids down inside mitochondria. Why is it useful that these happen in different compartments?
options: Keeping them apart stops new fatty acids from being broken down straight away, wasting energy.
Keeping them apart lets both processes use the same enzymes, which saves the cell from making extra proteins.
Keeping them apart means the fatty acids can be built and broken down at the same rate in each compartment.
Keeping them apart lets fatty acids leave the cell faster, because each compartment opens to the outside.

items.q: A student claims that because prokaryotes have no membrane-bound organelles, their insides have no organization at all. Which observation best refutes the claim?
options: Their DNA gathers in a nucleoid, and some have internal membrane sheets for photosynthesis.
Their cytoplasm contains ribosomes, which are made of rRNA and protein and build the cell's proteins.
Their plasma membrane contains transport proteins that control which substances enter and leave.
They are usually much smaller than eukaryotic cells, so substances reach each part of the cell by diffusion.

items.q: Order these compartments of an animal cell from most acidic to least acidic.
options: Lysosome interior (about pH 5)
Cytosol (about pH 7.2)
Mitochondrial matrix (about pH 7.8)

items.q: Chloroplasts hold their light-absorbing proteins in thylakoids, flattened membrane sacs piled into stacks. What advantage does this arrangement give?
options: It packs a large membrane area into the chloroplast, so it holds many more light-absorbing proteins.
It keeps light out of the stroma, so the reactions there can run in the dark at any time of day.
It lets the chloroplast take in water faster, because each thylakoid works like an aquaporin.
It makes the chloroplast smaller, so it can move to the cell surface where light is strongest.

items.q: Certain cells cannot make a working version of the lysosomal enzyme that breaks down a particular fat. Which outcome is expected in these cells?
options: That fat builds up inside their lysosomes, which swell, while other lysosomal digestion continues.
That fat is broken down in the cytosol instead, because the cytosolic enzymes take over the job.
Digestion in their lysosomes stops altogether, because lysosomes need each of their enzymes to work.
That fat leaks out of the lysosomes and is digested by the acidic contents of the cytosol.

items.q: Which are advantages that internal membranes give a eukaryotic cell? Select all that apply.
options: Different pH and other conditions can be kept in different organelles at the same time.
Opposing processes, such as building and breaking down a molecule, can be kept apart.
Membrane folds pack extra area for membrane proteins into a small space.
Molecules move between organelles faster than they would if the cell were one open space.
Each reaction in the cell can then run at the same pH and temperature.

items.q: A cell must keep a reaction's starting molecules at high concentration to make the reaction run fast. How can a membrane-bound compartment help, even in a large cell?
options: Transport proteins can gather the molecules into a small space, where their concentration stays high.
The compartment's membrane makes the molecules react without any enzyme being present.
The compartment lets the molecules diffuse faster, because water moves more quickly inside organelles.
The compartment raises the cell's surface area-to-volume ratio, so the whole cell becomes smaller.

items.q: In a diagram, a cell has DNA surrounded by a double membrane with pores, ribosomes on membranes nearby, and small acidic sacs. Which kind of cell is it, and why?
options: Eukaryotic, because its DNA is enclosed in a nucleus and it has membrane-bound organelles.
Prokaryotic, because its DNA is in a nucleoid and it has ribosomes for making proteins.
Prokaryotic, because its double membrane and pores show a cell wall around the DNA.
Eukaryotic, because it has ribosomes, which prokaryotic cells do not have.

items.q: Eukaryotic cells are usually 10 to 100 times wider than prokaryotic cells. Which claim best links this to compartments?
options: Internal membranes add working surface and keep reactions concentrated in small spaces, helping a large cell function.
Internal membranes raise the surface area-to-volume ratio of the outer membrane, so large cells exchange faster.
Large cells need compartments to hold extra water, which keeps them from bursting in hypotonic solutions.
Compartments make cells larger by adding membrane, so having organelles is what causes eukaryotic cells to be big.

items.q: Which feature in the table do mitochondria share with bacteria but not with the plant cell's cytoplasm?
options: Ribosomes of about 70 S, which streptomycin blocks
Chromosomes that are not loops, held inside a nucleus
A length of 10 to 100 micrometers, like the whole cell
New ones forming by ordinary cell division

items.q: Why is the streptomycin row evidence for the endosymbiotic theory?
options: A drug aimed at bacterial ribosomes also blocks the organelles' ribosomes, so theirs are bacteria-like.
The drug kills mitochondria and chloroplasts, showing that they are separate living bacteria inside the cell today.
Protein production in the cytoplasm is unaffected, showing that the cytoplasm came from a bacterium.
Streptomycin enters organelles more easily than cytoplasm, showing that organelles have bacterial membranes.

items.q: Some antibiotics that block bacterial ribosomes can cause side effects in human tissues when given at high doses for a long time. Based on the table, which tissues are most likely to be affected?

Tissues whose cells have no mitochondria, such as mature red blood cells, because they depend on bacterial-type ribosomes.
Tissues whose cells divide most often, because the drug blocks the 80 S ribosomes in their cytoplasm.
Tissues whose cells are largest, because larger cells contain more of the bacterial ribosomes the drug binds.

items.q: Which observations are evidence that chloroplasts descend from bacteria? Select all that apply.
options: Chloroplast DNA is circular.
Chloroplast ribosomes are about 70 S.
New chloroplasts form by splitting of existing ones.
Chloroplasts are surrounded by two membranes.
Chloroplasts are found in plant and algal cells but not in animal cells.
Chloroplasts contain a green substance that absorbs light.

items.q: By what percent did streptomycin reduce protein production in mitochondria?
In step 2 of the model, the bacterium is surrounded by two membranes. According to the model, where does the outer membrane come from?
options: The host cell's plasma membrane, which wrapped around the bacterium as it was taken in
The bacterium's cell wall, which turned into a membrane once it was inside
A second bacterium that was taken in at the same time and fused with the first
The host cell's nucleus, which sent a layer of its own envelope around the bacterium

items.q: According to the model, why do plant and algal cells have both mitochondria and chloroplasts, while animal cells have only mitochondria?
options: Mitochondria came first; a photosynthetic bacterium was later taken in by one line of those cells.
Chloroplasts were gained first, and animal cells later lost theirs while keeping their mitochondria.
Both were gained at the same moment, and animal cells later turned their chloroplasts into mitochondria.
Plant cells are larger, so they had room to take in two kinds of bacteria at once while animal cells did not.

items.q: Which new finding would most strongly support the model?
options: Mitochondrial DNA matches DNA of certain living bacteria better than it matches the cell's nuclear DNA.
Mitochondria are found in the cells of most eukaryotes, including animals, plants, fungi and many single-celled groups.
Mitochondria move around inside the cell along the cytoskeleton, toward regions that need more ATP.
Cells with more mitochondria use more oxygen than cells with fewer mitochondria in the same tissue.

items.q: A researcher removes every mitochondrion from a living yeast cell without killing it right away. If the model is correct, what is expected?
options: The cell cannot build new mitochondria, because mitochondria form only by splitting of existing ones.
The cell builds new mitochondria from its own membranes, because it has the genes to make them.
The cell makes new mitochondria within hours by folding its plasma membrane inward.
The cell takes in free-living bacteria from its surroundings and turns them into mitochondria.

items.q: Put the events of the endosymbiotic theory in the order the model shows them.
options: A host cell takes in an oxygen-using bacterium by wrapping its membrane around it.
The bacterium survives inside the host, enclosed by two membranes.
Over many generations the bacterium's descendants become mitochondria that divide inside the cell.
In one line of these cells, a photosynthetic bacterium is taken in and becomes the chloroplast.

items.q: What does the endosymbiotic theory propose?
options: Mitochondria and chloroplasts descend from free-living prokaryotes taken in by ancient host cells.
The nucleus formed when a large bacterium was swallowed by a smaller one and kept its DNA.
Mitochondria and chloroplasts formed from folds of the plasma membrane that pinched off inside the cell.
Prokaryotes descend from eukaryotic cells that lost their nucleus and organelles over time.

items.q: In the early partnership, the host cell gained a supply of ATP and the bacterium gained shelter and a steady supply of food molecules. How is this relationship best described?
options: Mutualism, a kind of symbiosis in which both partners benefit
A partnership in which the host benefits while the bacterium is harmed
Competition, because the two partners use the same food molecules
A short-term encounter, because the bacterium was digested soon after

items.q: Human mitochondrial DNA carries 37 genes. Free-living relatives of the bacteria that mitochondria came from carry more than 1,000. Most of the proteins inside a human mitochondrion are coded by genes in the nucleus. Which explanation fits these facts and the endosymbiotic theory?
options: Over a long time, most of the endosymbiont's genes were lost or moved into the host's nucleus.
Mitochondria had no more than 37 genes at any point, so they did not descend from bacteria.
The host cell's nucleus made the mitochondrion from scratch and gave it a few genes to keep.
Mitochondria still have over 1,000 genes, but most of them are hidden in the nucleus of the bacterium.

items.q: A student says, "Mitochondria are just bacteria that live in our cells today." Which evidence best shows this claim goes too far?
options: Mitochondria cannot survive outside a cell, and most of their proteins are coded by genes in the nucleus.
Mitochondria have two membranes, circular DNA and ribosomes that resemble bacterial ribosomes in size and drug sensitivity.
Mitochondria divide by splitting, the way bacteria divide by binary fission.
Mitochondria are about the same size as many bacteria, 1 to 10 micrometers long.

items.q: The outer membrane of the nuclear envelope is continuous with the membrane of the endoplasmic reticulum. How does this observation relate to the membrane infolding hypothesis?
options: It fits the hypothesis, because both could have formed from the same inward folds of the plasma membrane.
It proves the hypothesis, because no other known process could connect two separate membranes inside one cell.
It shows the nucleus came from an engulfed bacterium, because the envelope has two membranes.
It contradicts the hypothesis, because folded membranes would stay attached to the plasma membrane.

items.q: In biology, what does evolution mean?
options: Change in the inherited traits of populations over many generations
Change in a single organism's body during its own lifetime
Any change in the number of individuals in a population
Improvement of a species toward a more complex and more perfect final form

items.q: Nearly every eukaryote has mitochondria or traces of them, but only plants and algae have chloroplasts. What does this pattern suggest about common ancestry?
options: Eukaryotes share an ancestor that already had mitochondria; chloroplasts came later in one branch.
Each eukaryotic group took in its own mitochondria separately, so they share no common ancestor.
Plants and algae are older than animals and fungi, because they carry a larger number of organelles.
Chloroplasts were in the first eukaryote and were lost by each group except plants and algae.

items.q: Which features are found in prokaryotic cells? Select all that apply.
options: Ribosomes
A nucleus surrounded by a double membrane
Mitochondria
Endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi

items.q: A single-celled organism called Paulinella holds photosynthetic bodies that are larger than typical chloroplasts, still carry many more genes than chloroplasts do, and arose from a much more recent engulfing event. How does this organism bear on the endosymbiotic theory?
options: It shows the kind of event the theory describes can happen more than once, seen at an earlier stage.
